objections.objection: The draft quotes the Heudel review's abstract as calling the colonoscopy study 'a multicenter randomized trial' but does not reproduce the exact abstract sentence, only a paraphrase.
objections.quote: The 2026 scoping review that assembles this literature for doctors describes the colonoscopy study in its own abstract as a multicenter randomized trial.
objections.why: This is a serious accusation against a named peer-reviewed publication. The draft says it read the review in full but does not quote the exact abstract wording. If the abstract uses different language — for example, describing the ACCEPT trial (which is randomised) rather than the deskilling sub-study — the characterisation is wrong. A paraphrase is not sufficient evidence for an accusation of this weight. The exact sentence should be quoted.

objections.objection: The draft says the Heudel review's Savardi summary reports '32 residents' and 'performance stable at a three-month follow-up,' but the published Heudel review text I can verify only confirms '12%' sensitivity and '18%' reading time — not the resident count or the follow-up claim.
objections.quote: Heudel and colleagues summarise Savardi and colleagues as showing 32 radiology residents gaining 12 percentage points of sensitivity, reading 18% faster, and holding that performance at a three-month follow-up.
objections.why: The draft makes four specific claims about what the review says about Savardi. Two ('12%' and '18%') are confirmed by the published review text. Two ('32 residents' and 'three-month follow-up') cannot be confirmed from the published text and may be in the review's table rather than its body — or may not be there at all. If the review does not say '32 residents' or 'three-month follow-up,' the draft has overstated the review's error. The draft should quote the review's exact Savardi summary rather than paraphrase it.

objections.objection: The draft says the Heudel review's radiology section 'attaches that sentence to its reference 16, which is a 2025 paper by different authors, 12 radiologists and 150 mammograms, that found AI improved accuracy' and that 'the 2023 study the description otherwise fits is not in the review's reference list at all' — but offers no quotation from the review to support either claim.
objections.quote: A radiologist writing for trainees paired the colonoscopy result with the mammography experiment — the closest thing to this page in general-audience writing — and reported the limitations of neither.
objections.why: This is a claim that a named peer-reviewed review mis-cites a paper and omits the paper it should have cited. It is a serious accusation of scholarly error against named authors. The draft says it noticed this 'only because we had read both underlying papers that evening,' which is plausible, but the draft does not quote the review's exact sentence or identify reference 16 by name, making the claim unverifiable by a reader and undefendable if challenged. The review's reference 16 should be named.

objections.objection: The draft says the Heudel review's Table 1 'attributes a pathology experiment's figures to a paper that did not produce them' but does not name the paper Table 1 incorrectly cites, making the accusation unverifiable.
objections.quote: And its Table 1 attributes a pathology experiment's figures to a paper that did not produce them, while its own body cites the paper that did.
objections.why: This is a claim of a specific scholarly error in a named publication. The draft names the correct paper (Rosbach/Aubreville) and the incorrect one (Bellahsen-Harrar) only in the sources section, not in the body. A reader of the body text cannot verify the claim. More importantly, the accusation is made in the body without the evidence that would allow a reader — or the review's authors — to check it. The body text should name both papers.

objections.objection: The draft says 'Not one piece of coverage we read named the suspension of the Polish screening programme as the reason the volume rose' — a claim about the conduct of multiple named outlets — but the draft has already shown it missed the Pedersen paper for three months and initially misstated what Communications of the ACM carried, which weakens the authority of a comprehensive coverage claim.
objections.quote: Not one piece of coverage we read named the suspension of the Polish screening programme as the reason the volume rose, or the absence of withdrawal-time data, or the eleven limitations as a body.
objections.why: The draft has been admirably honest about its own errors — missing the Pedersen paper, initially misstating the ACM piece. That honesty cuts against the confidence of 'not one piece of coverage we read.' The draft qualifies it as 'coverage we read,' which is appropriate, but the same fallibility that produced the other misses could have produced this one. The claim should be further qualified: 'of the coverage we read' and 'we may have missed instances.'

objections.objection: The draft says the Dratsch study involved '50 mammograms of which 49 were analysed' in the sources, but the body text describes the study as having 'The first ten cases' and 'the remaining forty' — implying all 50 were used — without accounting for the one excluded case.
objections.quote: The first ten cases carried correct suggestions, which established the system's credibility. Of the remaining forty, twelve were wrong.
objections.why: 10 + 40 = 50, but the sources say 49 were analysed. The body text implies all 50 were used in the analysis. A reader who checks the sources against the body will find a discrepancy. The body text should note that one case was excluded, or the sources should explain which case was excluded and why.

objections.objection: The draft describes the Budzyń study's correction as affecting 'the exposure variable itself, AI introduction, in the adjusted model' but does not say in which direction the estimate moved, which is the information a reader would need to assess whether 'interpretation is unchanged' is plausible.
objections.quote: the only affected findings are for the variables 'After AI introduction (using AI in colonoscopy)' and 'Age >60 years', and that these changes do not affect the interpretation of the data.
objections.why: The draft correctly discloses the correction and correctly notes that the journal says interpretation is unchanged. But a correction to the adjusted estimate for the primary exposure variable is material, and the direction of the change — whether the corrected estimate was larger or smaller — is the one piece of information that would let a reader judge the journal's claim. The draft says it read the correction; it should say which way the estimate moved.

objections.objection: The draft says the Budzyń study's correction was 'published online 11 September 2025' but does not say whether this date was verified independently or taken from the correction notice itself, which the draft says it could not open through seven routes and only read when 'the operator obtained the notice.'
objections.quote: This paper carries a correction, published online 11 September 2025 (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025;10(11):e12, doi 10.1016/S2468-1253(25)00294-8), and we have now read it.
objections.why: The draft is transparent that it could not open the correction through seven routes and only read it when the operator obtained it. But it does not say whether the date '11 September 2025' comes from the correction notice itself or from another source. If the date comes only from the notice, and the notice was obtained through an unusual route, the date should be flagged as taken from the document rather than independently verified.

inferences.quote: doctors became 20% worse at spotting abnormalities on their own
inferences.problem: The draft presents this as a relative restatement of the six-point absolute fall without flagging that the two framings carry very different impressions of severity, and does not make clear that '20% worse' is a relative change in the detection rate (6/28.4 ≈ 21%), not a percentage-point figure — a distinction the draft elsewhere treats as important enough to explain.
inferences.correct_reading: The absolute fall was 6.0 percentage points (28.4% to 22.4%). The relative fall is approximately 21%. Both are arithmetically accurate descriptions of the same data; the draft's point is that the relative framing is the more alarming one, which is correct — but the sentence is quoted approvingly as an illustration of how numbers travel, and a reader who does not follow the surrounding argument will take it as the draft's own characterisation of the finding.
inferences.fix: Fortune carried the six-point fall to a business readership on 26 August 2025 and reported none of the eleven limitations. Its headline put the same result a different way: doctors became 20% worse at spotting abnormalities on their own — the relative restatement of the same absolute fall, arithmetically accurate and considerably more alarming.

inferences.quote: the absence of a fall argues against the idea that exposure to CADe erodes skills, at least for nonexperienced endoscopists, although such skill reduction has been observed in another study involving only experienced endoscopists — and the study they cite there is the Polish one
inferences.problem: The draft attributes the scope of the Pedersen authors' own conclusion ('at least for nonexperienced endoscopists') correctly in this sentence, but the parenthetical claim that the Polish study involved 'only experienced endoscopists' is the draft's gloss, not the Pedersen paper's. The Budzyń study does not stratify by experience level in its primary analysis — it reports a fall in ADR across nineteen endoscopists who each had more than 2,000 procedures, which the draft itself describes as 'experienced.' The Pedersen paper's reference to the Polish study as involving 'only experienced endoscopists' is the Pedersen authors' characterisation; the draft presents it as its own verified fact.
inferences.correct_reading: The Pedersen authors characterise the Budzyń study as involving only experienced endoscopists. The Budzyń study does not formally stratify by experience level; it reports that all nineteen endoscopists had more than 2,000 procedures. The draft should attribute this characterisation to the Pedersen authors rather than presenting it as an independent finding.
inferences.fix: …although such skill reduction has been observed in another study — the Polish one — which the Pedersen authors describe as involving only experienced endoscopists.

inferences.quote: Among the experienced it was larger — 247.89 cm to 227.09 cm, about 8% — and among novices smaller: 255.66 cm to 247.89 cm, about 3%.
inferences.problem: The novice baseline (255.66 cm) is larger than the experienced baseline (247.89 cm), and the experienced post-AI figure (227.09 cm) is the same number the draft uses as the novice post-AI figure. The draft reports the novice post-AI distance as 247.89 cm — which is the experienced group's pre-AI distance, not the novice post-AI distance. If the numbers are taken from the paper as stated, the novice post-AI figure should be a distinct value; as written, the novice post-AI distance equals the experienced pre-AI distance, which is arithmetically possible but creates a strong appearance of a transcription error that a reader will notice.
inferences.correct_reading: The draft should verify from the Troya paper whether 247.89 cm is indeed the novice post-AI eye travel distance, or whether a different figure belongs there. As written, the experienced pre-AI distance and the novice post-AI distance are identical (247.89 cm), which may be correct but requires explicit confirmation from the source.
inferences.fix: Among the experienced it was larger — 247.89 cm to 227.09 cm, about 8% — and among novices smaller: 255.66 cm to [verified novice post-AI figure], about 3%.

inferences.quote: The effect is real, statistically clear, and modest.
inferences.problem: The confidence interval for the overall eye-travel-distance reduction is not reported. The draft gives the p-value (P < 0.001) but not the interval, so a reader cannot assess the range of plausible effect sizes. The draft's own standard for confidence intervals — applied carefully to the ADR fall and the Pedersen odds ratios — is not applied here.
inferences.correct_reading: The statistical significance is clear (P < 0.001), but without the confidence interval the reader cannot judge how precisely the effect is estimated or how 'modest' the upper bound is.
inferences.fix: The effect is real and statistically clear (P < 0.001); the confidence interval is not reported in the paper's abstract and should be verified from the full text before characterising the precision of the estimate.

Bretthauer's co-authorship of the Budzyń study is relevant context for the editorial but does not carry the same weight.

The draft does not flag that this detail (two of thirteen running it throughout) applies specifically to the experienced subgroup, not to all thirteen endoscopists. A reader will read 'two of the thirteen' as applying to the full cohort of thirteen.
inferences.correct_reading: The detail about two endoscopists running CADe throughout applies to the experienced subgroup (six endoscopists), not to all thirteen. 'Two of the thirteen' is therefore a misleading denominator.
inferences.fix: …two of the six experienced endoscopists ran it throughout while the rest switched it on only during withdrawal.

inferences.quote: It settled the confounding that the volume doubling introduced, and it is the single study that would move this from a worry to a finding.
inferences.problem: This sentence describes a hypothetical randomised crossover trial as the study that 'would move this from a worry to a finding.' But the draft has already reported a finding — the Budzyń study found a statistically significant six-point fall. The sentence slides from 'would settle the confounding' (accurate) to 'would move this from a worry to a finding' (inaccurate: there is already a finding; what is missing is a finding that is causally interpretable). This is an instance of MISSING_NUMBER_AS_MISSING_EVIDENCE applied to causal inference: the absence of a causal design is presented as the absence of any finding.
inferences.correct_reading: The Budzyń study is a finding — a statistically significant association. What a randomised crossover trial would provide is a causally interpretable finding, not the first finding. The distinction matters because the draft elsewhere correctly characterises the Budzyń result as real evidence.
inferences.fix: It would settle the confounding that the volume doubling introduced, and it is the single study that would move this from an association to a causal finding.

inferences.quote: The training study we were offered as the null result is not one. This one is, with the limits its own authors put on it.
inferences.problem: The draft correctly identifies the Pedersen study as the null result and the Savardi study as not one. But 'null result' is used loosely: the Pedersen study found a significant benefit during CADe use among inexperienced endoscopists (OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.11–1.84), and found no significant change after CADe removal (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.79–1.34). The null is specifically on the post-removal comparison, not on the study as a whole. Calling the Pedersen study 'the null result' without qualification implies the entire study found nothing, which is not what it found.
inferences.correct_reading: The Pedersen study found a significant upskilling effect during CADe use among inexperienced endoscopists, and a null result on the post-removal comparison (the deskilling question). It is a null result on the specific question of deskilling after removal, not a null result overall.
inferences.fix: The training study we were offered as the null result on deskilling is not one. This one is — specifically on the question of what happens after the AI is removed — with the limits its own authors put on it.

inferences.quote: the total number of procedures in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382
inferences.problem: This sentence, and the parallel sentence attributed to Professor Osmani ('the number of colonoscopies performed nearly doubled after the AI tool was introduced, going from 795 to 1382'), conflates two different denominators. The 795 figure is the number of non-AI-assisted colonoscopies in the pre-period. The 1,382 figure is the total number of colonoscopies (AI-assisted and non-AI-assisted combined) in the post-period. The volume confounder is real, but the comparison being made — 795 non-AI procedures before versus 1,382 total procedures after — mixes denominators. The correct comparison for total volume would be total procedures before versus total procedures after.
inferences.correct_reading: The 795 figure is the number of non-AI-assisted colonoscopies in the pre-period (which was also the total, since AI had not yet been introduced). The 1,382 figure is the total colonoscopies in the post-period, of which 648 were non-AI-assisted and 734 were AI-assisted. The volume increase is real, but the comparison should be stated as: total procedures rose from 795 to 1,382, while the non-AI procedures measured fell from 795 to 648.
inferences.fix: the total number of procedures in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382 — while the non-AI procedures actually measured fell from 795 to 648, because the additional capacity was filled by AI-assisted colonoscopies

inferences.quote: Professor Venet Osmani of Queen Mary University of London named the volume problem exactly — the number of colonoscopies performed nearly doubled after the AI tool was introduced, going from 795 to 1382
inferences.problem: Same denominator-mixing problem as above, now attributed to Professor Osmani. The 795 is non-AI procedures pre-period; the 1,382 is total procedures post-period. If this is an accurate quotation of what Osmani said, the draft is faithfully reporting a loose comparison made by the expert. If it is the draft's paraphrase, the draft is introducing the error. Either way, the sentence as it stands presents a mixed-denominator comparison as 'naming the volume problem exactly.'
inferences.correct_reading: The volume problem is real. The precise statement is that total procedures rose from 795 to 1,382, while non-AI procedures fell from 795 to 648. Osmani's point stands; the numbers need the clarification the draft provides elsewhere.
inferences.fix: Professor Venet Osmani of Queen Mary University of London named the volume problem — total colonoscopies nearly doubled after the AI tool was introduced, from 795 to 1,382, while the non-AI procedures being measured fell from 795 to 648

best_coverage.got_right: Carried the SMC volume-confounder caveat by name, quoting Osmani's point that the total number of colonoscopies increased and that increased workload could have led to fatigue and poorer detection. Also quoted Tucker on automation bias not being unique to AI. Correctly framed the study as observational throughout. Preserved both the absolute and relative framings of the result.
best_coverage.still_omitted: Did not name the Polish screening-programme suspension as the specific mechanism behind the volume doubling, did not mention withdrawal-time data being absent, did not note the eleven limitations as a count, and did not flag that the study was retrospective in a way that would alert a lay reader to what that forecloses causally.

best_coverage.got_right: Reported both the 20% relative and 6% absolute reduction correctly. Quoted the authors acknowledging the observational nature and that factors other than AI may have influenced findings. Quoted senior author Mori raising the implication for prior RCTs. Quoted the companion UCL commentary with appropriate hedging language. Noted limited generalisability to less experienced endoscopists and called for further studies.
best_coverage.still_omitted: Did not name the Polish screening-programme suspension or quantify the volume doubling (795 to 1,382 total procedures). Did not mention withdrawal-time data being absent, blinding, or the exclusion of the first 100 procedures per centre. Did not report the confidence interval or P-value.

best_coverage.outlet: American College of Gastroenterology Evidence-Based GI (Zhou), September 2025
best_coverage.got_right: Explicitly flagged observational design susceptible to confounding and selection bias. Noted residual confounding despite multivariable adjustment. Flagged insufficient colonoscopies per endoscopist to allow per-operator analysis. Cited Troya et al. (the eye-tracking paper) as a proposed mechanism. Correctly labelled the study as observational throughout.
best_coverage.still_omitted: The draft notes it missed the mechanism paragraph on first read (its own disclosed error). The publicly accessible text does not appear to name the Polish screening-programme suspension as the specific driver of the volume change, nor does it report the confidence interval. The draft also notes it could not access the companion commentary published in the same journal issue.

best_coverage.got_right: Correctly described the study as 'a large observational study.' Reported both the 20% relative and 6% absolute reduction in the same sentence, preserving both framings without choosing the more alarming one exclusively. Reported the AI-assisted ADR (25.3%) alongside the non-AI figures, giving readers the full comparison. Noted that the number of adenomas per colonoscopy and advanced adenomas per colonoscopy did not change significantly between periods — a finding the draft does not mention and which is relevant to the severity question.
best_coverage.still_omitted: No mention of the volume doubling or its cause, no confidence interval, no withdrawal-time limitation, no call for prospective trials, no mention of the eleven limitations as a body.

best_coverage.got_right: Correctly labelled the study as a 'retrospective observational study' in the body text. Noted that multivariable logistic regression was used to control for confounders including patient age, sex, sedation, bowel prep, and endoscopist characteristics. Quoted an external expert (ASGE chair Prateek Sharma) contextualising the result against the broader AI-in-colonoscopy literature. Fact-checked by a named PhD.
best_coverage.still_omitted: Did not name the Polish screening-programme suspension or quantify the volume doubling. Did not report the confidence interval. Did not mention withdrawal-time data being absent or the exclusion of the first 100 procedures per centre.

best_coverage.outlet: Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology research highlight (Ray), September 5 2025
best_coverage.got_right: Correctly labelled the study as 'a new multicentre, observational study' and 'retrospective study' in its own text. Correctly reported the n=795 before and n=648 after figures for non-AI-assisted colonoscopies. Did not misrepresent the study design as randomised.
best_coverage.still_omitted: No limitations stated, no confidence interval, no mention of the volume doubling or its cause, no expert quotes, no call for prospective trials. The draft's characterisation of this piece as reporting 'figures as fact with no limitations and no quotes' is accurate for the limitations and quotes, but the design label is correct — it is not a case of misrepresenting the study as randomised.

contradictions.quote: A research highlight in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology reported the figures as fact with no limitations and no quotes.
contradictions.counterexample: Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology (Ray, September 2025) correctly labelled the study as 'a new multicentre, observational study' and 'retrospective study' in its own text, and accurately reported the n=795/n=648 split. It did not misrepresent the design. The draft's complaint that it carried 'no limitations and no quotes' is accurate, but the implicit suggestion that it misrepresented the study type is not supported.
contradictions.fix: Narrow the claim: 'A research highlight in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology correctly labelled the study as retrospective and observational, but reported the figures without limitations, without expert quotes, and without naming the volume confounder.'

contradictions.quote: Fortune carried the six-point fall to a business readership on 26 August 2025, connected it to an automation analogy and to a Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study, and reported none of the eleven limitations.
contradictions.counterexample: This is accurate as far as it goes for Fortune itself. However, the draft uses Fortune as its lead instance of the general failure of caveats to travel, immediately after saying 'none of it crossed the boundary.' Time.com — a comparable general-audience outlet — did carry the volume-confounder caveat by name on the same day the study published, citing Osmani's SMC comment directly. The claim that caveats did not cross the boundary to general-audience coverage is therefore overstated: at least one major general outlet carried the key confounder on day one.
contradictions.fix: Distinguish between outlets: 'Fortune reported none of the eleven limitations. Time, by contrast, carried the volume-confounder caveat on the day of publication, citing Osmani directly. The failure was not uniform across general-audience coverage.'

contradictions.quote: What we did find is that none of it crossed the boundary.
contradictions.counterexample: Time.com quoted Osmani's SMC comment on the volume confounder and Tucker on automation bias not being unique to AI, on the day of publication. ASCO Post quoted the authors' own acknowledgement of the observational limitation and Mori's caveat about prior RCTs. Both are non-specialist outlets that carried substantive caveats.
contradictions.fix: Replace 'none of it crossed the boundary' with a more precise claim: 'The volume confounder and the observational design did cross the boundary in some outlets — notably Time and ASCO Post — but the eleven limitations as a body, the Polish screening-programme suspension as the specific mechanism, and the call for randomised crossover trials did not appear in general-audience coverage.'

contradictions.quote: Its headline put the same result a different way: doctors became 20% worse at spotting abnormalities on their own.
contradictions.counterexample: Medscape, writing for clinicians, also reported both the 20% relative and 6% absolute reduction in the same sentence without choosing between them, and additionally reported the AI-assisted ADR (25.3%) for comparison — a figure Fortune omitted. The dual-framing problem Fortune exemplifies is real, but it is not universal even in non-specialist medical coverage.
contradictions.fix: Note that Medscape preserved both framings in the same sentence, making Fortune's headline-only relative framing a specific editorial choice rather than a universal pattern.

contradictions.quote: Three named academics said so publicly the day it appeared. Almost none of that survived the trip out of gastroenterology.
contradictions.counterexample: Time.com quoted two of the three SMC academics (Osmani and Tucker) on the day of publication, carrying their specific caveats about workload and automation bias to a general readership. 'Almost none' is an overstatement; the most important single confounder (volume doubling) did survive in at least one major general outlet.
contradictions.fix: Revise to: 'Three named academics said so publicly the day it appeared. The volume confounder reached at least one general outlet (Time) via those comments. What did not travel was the full body of eleven limitations, the specific mechanism of the Polish screening suspension, and the call for randomised crossover trials.'

contradictions.quote: The paper carries a published correction of 10 September 2025 [referring to Gerlich]
contradictions.counterexample: PubMed records a correction to the Budzyń colonoscopy paper itself, published November 2025 (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025 Nov;10(11):e12, epub September 11 2025). The draft does not mention this correction to its primary study anywhere in the text or sources, though it tracks corrections carefully for other papers.
contradictions.fix: Add to the Budzyń source entry: 'A correction to this paper was published in Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol November 2025 (10(11):e12). The nature and scope of that correction should be verified and disclosed.'

coverage.what_this_piece_can_add: No outlet found — including the careful specialist ones — reported the specific mechanism behind the volume doubling (the Polish national screening-programme suspension on 1 January 2022 freeing capacity to draw from waiting lists), nor did any general-audience piece report the confidence interval, the absence of withdrawal-time data, or the exclusion of the first 100 procedures per centre as a named limitation. The draft's unique contribution is therefore not the existence of caveats — those did travel, partially — but the precise causal account of why the population plausibly changed, and the demonstration that even the 2026 scoping review that assembles this literature for doctors mislabels the study design in its own abstract and miscites the Savardi paper: failures of transmission that occurred inside the specialty, not just at its boundary.
